concepts.def: The monomer from which polypeptides are built. Every amino acid has a central alpha carbon atom to which four things are bonded: an amine group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and an R-group. The amine group, carboxyl group and hydrogen are the same in every amino acid; only the R-group differs.

The central carbon atom of an amino acid, which carries the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Because the amine and carboxyl groups are on the same carbon, the alpha carbon becomes part of the repeating backbone of a polypeptide when amino acids are linked.

The variable side group attached to the alpha carbon of an amino acid. Each of the 20 amino acids coded for in the genetic code has a different R-group, and it is the R-group alone that distinguishes one amino acid from another.

The two functional groups present in every amino acid. The amine group (–NH₂) is a nitrogen atom bonded to the alpha carbon and to two hydrogen atoms; the carboxyl group (–COOH) is a carbon atom bonded to the alpha carbon, double-bonded to one oxygen and bonded to a hydroxyl group. The amine group can bind a hydrogen ion to become –NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl group can dissociate to –COO⁻.

The reaction that links two amino acids: the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amine group of the other, forming a peptide bond and releasing one molecule of water. Word equation: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. Repeating the reaction adds further amino acids one at a time, so a chain of n amino acids is formed with the release of n − 1 water molecules.

The covalent bond formed by a condensation reaction between the carbon of the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the nitrogen of the amine group of the next. In a polypeptide the peptide bonds join the alpha carbons into a continuous backbone; the R-groups project from the backbone and are not part of the bond.

Two amino acids linked by a single peptide bond. A generalized dipeptide has a free amine group at one end, a free carboxyl group at the other end, two alpha carbons each carrying a hydrogen and an R-group, and the peptide bond (–CO–NH–) between them.

An amino acid that cannot be synthesized in the body and must therefore be obtained from protein in food. A diet that lacks any essential amino acid limits the synthesis of proteins that contain it, however much other protein is eaten.

The 20 different amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code and assembled into polypeptides by ribosomes. Because a peptide chain can contain any number of amino acids, from a few to thousands, and the amino acids can be in any order, the number of possible different polypeptides is effectively infinite: for a chain of n amino acids there are 20ⁿ possible sequences.

A chain of many amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Examples span a wide range of lengths: the two chains of insulin have 21 and 30 amino acids (51 in total); lysozyme, an enzyme in tears and egg white, has 129; the alpha and beta chains of haemoglobin have 141 and 146; each polypeptide of collagen has around 1000; and titin, a muscle protein, has more than 30 000. A protein consists of one or more polypeptides.

A change in the three-dimensional shape (conformation) of a protein caused by high temperature or by a pH away from the range the protein is adapted to, so that the protein can no longer carry out its function. Heat makes the molecule vibrate more strongly, breaking the weak bonds that hold the folded shape; a change in pH alters the charges on the protein and so disrupts the bonds that depend on them. Peptide bonds are not broken, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged, but the change of shape is in most cases permanent.

A non-polar R-group that does not form hydrogen bonds with water and is therefore not attracted to it. In an aqueous environment, amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups tend to be positioned away from water. Because R-groups determine the properties of assembled polypeptides, the pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic R-groups along a chain largely decides how it folds.

concepts.term: Hydrophilic R-group (polar or charged; acidic or basic)
concepts.def: An R-group that is attracted to water. Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, forming hydrogen bonds with water, or charged. Charged R-groups are acidic, if they contain a carboxyl group that can dissociate to release a hydrogen ion and become negatively charged, or basic, if they contain an amine group that can bind a hydrogen ion and become positively charged.

The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, from the amine end to the carboxyl end, held together by peptide bonds. The primary structure determines every higher level of structure: the identity and precise position of each amino acid decides where the chain can coil, pleat and fold, and which R-groups end up close enough to bond.

The three-dimensional shape adopted by a protein. Because it is determined by the amino acid sequence, the conformation of a given protein is precise, predictable and repeatable: every molecule of a protein with the same primary structure folds into the same shape, despite the complexity of that shape.

Regular coiling or pleating of parts of a polypeptide chain, stabilized by hydrogen bonds at regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the backbone. The R-groups are not involved. The two main forms are the alpha helix and the beta-pleated sheet, and a single polypeptide may contain both, joined by less regular regions.

A secondary structure in which the polypeptide backbone is coiled into a right-handed spiral, held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O group of each peptide bond and the N–H group of the peptide bond four amino acids further along the chain. The R-groups project outwards from the helix.

A secondary structure in which two or more lengths of polypeptide (strands) lie side by side and are held together by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbones of neighbouring strands, giving a pleated sheet with the R-groups projecting above and below it.

The overall three-dimensional folding of a whole polypeptide, including its regions of secondary structure, into its functional conformation. It is held by interactions between R-groups that the folding brings close together: hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups, ionic bonds between oppositely charged R-groups, disulfide covalent bonds between pairs of cysteines, and hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R-groups.

A covalent bond formed between the sulfur atoms of the R-groups of two cysteines that lie close together in the folded polypeptide (or in two different polypeptides). It is much stronger than the other interactions that hold tertiary structure and is not broken by moderate heating or by changes in pH, but it can be broken by reducing agents.

An attraction between a positively charged and a negatively charged R-group. Amine groups in R-groups become positively charged by binding hydrogen ions and carboxyl groups in R-groups become negatively charged by dissociation of hydrogen ions; the charged groups can then form ionic bonds. Because the charges depend on the binding and release of hydrogen ions, a change in pH can remove them and break the ionic bonds.

The association of non-polar R-groups with one another away from water. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other rather than to non-polar groups, so non-polar R-groups are excluded from the water and end up packed together; this helps hold the tertiary structure of a protein in an aqueous environment.

concepts.term: Hydrophobic core of a globular protein
concepts.def: In a protein that is soluble in water, the amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups are clustered in the centre of the folded molecule, away from the surrounding water, while amino acids with hydrophilic R-groups are mainly on the surface, where they interact with water and keep the protein in solution.

A protein embedded in a membrane. It has one or more regions in which the amino acids have hydrophobic R-groups; these regions sit within the hydrophobic centre of the phospholipid bilayer and anchor the protein in the membrane, while regions with hydrophilic R-groups project into the aqueous solution on either side.

The association of two or more polypeptides, each with its own tertiary structure, into a single functional protein. The polypeptides are held together by the same kinds of interaction as tertiary structure. Insulin (two polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds) and collagen (three polypeptides wound around each other) have quaternary structure; a protein made of a single polypeptide does not.

A conjugated protein contains one or more non-polypeptide components (prosthetic groups) in addition to its polypeptides: haemoglobin is conjugated because each of its four polypeptides carries a haem group, which is not made of amino acids and contains an iron ion. A non-conjugated protein consists of polypeptides only: insulin and collagen are non-conjugated proteins.

A technique in which a sample is frozen very rapidly and imaged with an electron microscope, allowing the structure of single protein molecules, and of proteins interacting with other molecules, to be worked out. It illustrates that technology allows the imaging of structures that would be impossible to observe with the unaided senses, and so extends what can be known.

A protein whose polypeptide(s) fold into a compact, rounded shape. Globular proteins are generally soluble in water, with hydrophilic R-groups on the surface, and their precise three-dimensional shape lets them bind specifically to other molecules: insulin is a globular protein whose shape allows it to bind to insulin receptors on target cells, so that it can act as a hormone carried in the blood.

A protein with a long, narrow, elongated shape. Fibrous proteins are generally insoluble in water and have structural roles: collagen consists of three polypeptides wound together into a rope-like triple helix, and many collagen molecules are linked into fibres that give tendons, ligaments, skin and bone high tensile strength.

mcqs.q: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?
options: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.
The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same structure as a molecule of ammonia.
mcqs.specStatementText: The parts of any amino acid
mcqs.explain: This is the generalized structure of an amino acid: a central alpha carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20 amino acids.
rationales: This is the generalized structure of an amino acid: a central alpha carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20 amino acids.

A student who takes the fully drawn groups to be the variable parts picks this. In fact it is the other way round: the amine group, carboxyl group and hydrogen are the same in every amino acid, and only the R-group differs.
A student who writes an amino acid as NH₂–COOH picks this. In fact both groups are attached to the alpha carbon, which sits between them and also carries a hydrogen and the R-group.

A student who carries ammonia's three hydrogens over to the amine group picks this. In fact one of the nitrogen's bonds is to the alpha carbon, so the amine group is –NH₂; it becomes –NH₃⁺ only when it binds a hydrogen ion.

mcqs.q: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?
options: A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.
The amine group of one amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group of the other, and no water is released.
mcqs.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
mcqs.explain: This is the condensation reaction: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group, and one molecule of water is released.
rationales: A student who confuses condensation with hydrolysis picks this. In fact water is a product: a hydroxyl group from the carboxyl group and a hydrogen from the amine group are removed and combine to form the water that is released.

This is the condensation reaction: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group, and one molecule of water is released.

A student who assumes the distinctive R-groups must do the chemistry picks this. In fact the R-groups take no part in the reaction; the peptide bond is in the backbone, between a carboxyl group and an amine group.

A student who thinks the link between amino acids is a hydrogen bond picks this. In fact the peptide bond is a covalent C–N bond formed by a condensation reaction between the carboxyl group and the amine group, and one molecule of water is released as it forms.

mcqs.q: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?
options: 150 released
300 released
149 released
149 consumed
mcqs.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
mcqs.explain: Each condensation reaction links two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one molecule of water. Joining 150 amino acids into one chain needs 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.
rationales: A student who counts one water molecule per amino acid picks this. In fact one water molecule is released per peptide bond, and 150 amino acids are joined by 149 peptide bonds, because the two ends of the chain are unreacted.

A student who counts both the amine and the carboxyl group of every amino acid as releasing water picks this. In fact one peptide bond uses one carboxyl group and one amine group together and releases a single water molecule, so the total is 149.

Each condensation reaction links two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one molecule of water. Joining 150 amino acids into one chain needs 149 peptide bonds, so 149 water molecules are released.

A student who thinks water is a reactant in condensation picks this. In fact water is a product: it is formed from the –OH of a carboxyl group and the –H of an amine group and released, so 149 molecules are produced, not used up.

mcqs.q: What is meant by an essential amino acid?
options: One that the body needs in larger quantities than the non-essential amino acids.
One of the 20 amino acids, all of which must be supplied by the protein in the diet.
One that is found in animal protein but is absent from all plant-based foods.
One that cannot be synthesized in the body and must be obtained from food.
mcqs.specStatementText: Which amino acids must come from food
mcqs.explain: This is the definition: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids.
rationales: A student who reads essential in its everyday sense of important picks this. In fact the term says nothing about quantity: an essential amino acid is one that cannot be synthesized in the body and so must be obtained from food.

A student who thinks every amino acid has to come from food picks this. In fact only the essential amino acids must come from food; the non-essential ones can be made in the body from other amino acids.

A student who believes plant proteins contain no essential amino acids picks this. In fact plant proteins contain essential amino acids, although a single plant protein may be low in one or more of them; the definition concerns the body's inability to make them.
This is the definition: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids.

mcqs.q: A chemist makes tripeptides using only four different amino acids. Each of the three positions in a chain can hold any of the four amino acids. How many different tripeptides are possible?
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the variety of peptide chains is endless
mcqs.explain: Each of the three positions can independently hold any of the four amino acids, and amino acids can be repeated, so the number of sequences is 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64. With 20 amino acids and long chains the same reasoning gives an effectively infinite variety.
rationales: A student who assumes an amino acid cannot be used twice in a chain calculates 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. In fact amino acids can be repeated, so each position is an independent choice of four, giving 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

Each of the three positions can independently hold any of the four amino acids, and amino acids can be repeated, so the number of sequences is 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64. With 20 amino acids and long chains the same reasoning gives an effectively infinite variety.
A student who multiplies the number of amino acids by the chain length picks 4 × 3 = 12. In fact the choices at the three positions multiply together, so the number is 4³ = 64, not 4 × 3.

A student who puts the numbers the wrong way round calculates 3⁴ = 81. In fact the base is the number of amino acids available at each position and the power is the number of positions, so the answer is 4³ = 64.

mcqs.q: Why is the number of different possible polypeptides described as effectively infinite?
options: The 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order, but each amino acid can be used only once in a given chain.
There are very many combinations of amino acids, and the order of the amino acids does not affect the protein.
Chains can be of any length, and the 20 amino acids can occur in any order and be used any number of times.
Each extra amino acid added to a chain adds 20 to the number of different polypeptides that are possible.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the variety of peptide chains is endless
mcqs.explain: Twenty amino acids are coded for in the genetic code, peptide chains can have any number of amino acids from a few to thousands, and the amino acids can be in any order. The number of possible sequences, 20ⁿ for a chain of n amino acids, is therefore effectively infinite.
rationales: A student who pictures a polypeptide as a rearrangement of the 20 amino acids picks this. In fact any amino acid can occur any number of times, which is how chains of thousands of amino acids are possible.

A student who treats a polypeptide as a mixture of ingredients picks this. In fact the order matters: each different sequence is a different polypeptide with a different shape, which is a large part of why the variety is so great.

Twenty amino acids are coded for in the genetic code, peptide chains can have any number of amino acids from a few to thousands, and the amino acids can be in any order. The number of possible sequences, 20ⁿ for a chain of n amino acids, is therefore effectively infinite.
A student who adds rather than multiplies picks this. In fact each extra position multiplies the number of possible sequences by 20, so the total is 20ⁿ, which grows far faster than 20 × n.

mcqs.q: When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?
options: Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.
Heat has changed their shape temporarily, and they will refold as soon as the egg white cools.
Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
mcqs.explain: This is denaturation. Heat makes the molecules vibrate more, breaking the bonds that maintain the three-dimensional shape; the unfolded chains tangle with one another, which is why the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.
rationales: A student who thinks denaturation breaks the protein down picks this. In fact the covalent peptide bonds are unaffected by cooking temperatures; it is the weak bonds holding the folded shape that break, so the sequence is intact but the shape is lost.

A student who uses everyday language about heat killing things picks this. In fact proteins are molecules and cannot be killed; they have been denatured, meaning their conformation has changed so that they no longer function or dissolve.

A student who expects denaturation to reverse picks this. In fact denaturation is in most cases permanent: a cooked egg white does not become clear and liquid again when it cools, because the unfolded chains do not refold correctly.

This is denaturation. Heat makes the molecules vibrate more, breaking the bonds that maintain the three-dimensional shape; the unfolded chains tangle with one another, which is why the egg white becomes an insoluble solid.

mcqs.q: An enzyme's activity at its optimum pH of 7 was 100 units. One sample was placed at pH 2 for 10 minutes, then returned to pH 7: its activity was 4 units after 1 hour and 4 units after 24 hours, and its polypeptide chains were found to be intact. A second sample was cooled to 5 °C for 10 minutes, then returned to 37 °C: its activity was 100 units. What do these results show?
options: The low pH denatured the enzyme, changing its conformation in a way that was not reversed at pH 7, whereas the low temperature did not denature it.
Both treatments denatured the enzyme, but the denaturation caused by cooling was reversed when the sample was warmed again.
The acid-treated enzyme was only temporarily denatured and would have regained full activity if left for longer at pH 7.
The acid hydrolysed the peptide bonds of the enzyme, so its polypeptide chains were broken into separate amino acids.
mcqs.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
mcqs.explain: The pH 2 sample lost almost all activity and did not recover even after 24 hours at the optimum pH, while its chains stayed intact: its shape had changed permanently, which is denaturation. The cooled sample regained full activity, so its conformation was unchanged.
rationales: The pH 2 sample lost almost all activity and did not recover even after 24 hours at the optimum pH, while its chains stayed intact: its shape had changed permanently, which is denaturation. The cooled sample regained full activity, so its conformation was unchanged.

A student who thinks both sides of the temperature graph are explained by denaturation picks this. In fact low temperature does not change a protein's shape; it only slows molecular movement, so full recovery on warming shows the enzyme was not denatured.

A student who expects a protein to refold once conditions are restored picks this. In fact the activity was the same after 1 hour and after 24 hours, showing no recovery; denaturation is in most cases permanent.

A student who thinks denaturation breaks peptide bonds picks this. In fact the chains were found to be intact, so the loss of activity was due to a change of shape, not to breakdown of the primary structure.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the R-groups of amino acids is correct?
options: Every hydrophilic R-group must carry a charge; a polar R-group that is uncharged is classed as hydrophobic.
Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, or charged, and charged R-groups are acidic or basic.
An acidic R-group carries a positive charge, because an acid is a substance that contains hydrogen ions.
R-groups have little effect on a polypeptide, whose properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
mcqs.explain: R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic. Hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged; a charged R-group is acidic if its carboxyl group has dissociated to become negative, or basic if its amine group has bound a hydrogen ion to become positive.
rationales: A student who equates hydrophilic with charged picks this. In fact polar R-groups form hydrogen bonds with water and are hydrophilic even though they carry no overall charge; hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged.

R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic. Hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged; a charged R-group is acidic if its carboxyl group has dissociated to become negative, or basic if its amine group has bound a hydrogen ion to become positive.

A student who links acid with H⁺ and so with positive charge picks this. In fact an acidic R-group releases its hydrogen ion and is left negatively charged; it is the basic R-group that binds a hydrogen ion and becomes positive.

A student who sees the fully drawn amine and carboxyl groups as the important chemistry picks this. In fact those groups are used up in peptide bonds to make a backbone common to all polypeptides; it is the R-groups that determine the properties of the assembled polypeptide.

mcqs.q: Thousands of copies of the same enzyme are synthesized in a cell, and every copy has the same three-dimensional shape. Why?
options: The ribosome and Golgi apparatus mould each polypeptide into the shape the cell needs after it has been synthesized.
Every copy contains the same set of amino acids, and the order in which they occur has no effect at all on the final shape.
The sequence of amino acids, each in its precise position, determines the conformation, so folding is repeatable.
Only the few amino acids that form the active site affect the shape, and these are the same in every copy.
mcqs.explain: The primary structure determines the three-dimensional shape: the R-groups in their exact positions can form only one set of bonds, so every polypeptide with that sequence folds the same way. Proteins therefore have precise, predictable and repeatable structures.
rationales: A student who thinks a cell structure imposes the shape picks this. In fact the chain folds according to its own sequence; the ribosome joins the amino acids and the Golgi apparatus modifies proteins, but neither determines the conformation.

A student who treats a polypeptide as a mixture of ingredients picks this. In fact the shape depends on the sequence, not just the composition; the same amino acids in a different order would fold into a different shape.

The primary structure determines the three-dimensional shape: the R-groups in their exact positions can form only one set of bonds, so every polypeptide with that sequence folds the same way. Proteins therefore have precise, predictable and repeatable structures.

A student who sees the rest of the enzyme as filler picks this. In fact the precise position of every amino acid in the sequence contributes to the conformation, and the copies match because their whole sequences are identical.

mcqs.q: What stabilizes the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?
options: Hydrogen bonds between the R-groups of amino acids brought close together by folding.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.
Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
mcqs.specStatementText: Coils and pleats in the backbone (HL)
mcqs.explain: Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding in regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the polypeptide backbone.
rationales: A student who attaches every bond in a protein to R-groups picks this. In fact the R-groups project outwards from helices and sheets and take no part; the hydrogen bonds of secondary structure are between backbone groups.

A student who applies tertiary-structure bonding to secondary structure picks this. In fact disulfide bonds are between cysteine R-groups and belong to tertiary structure; helices and sheets depend on backbone hydrogen bonds.

A student who thinks peptide bonds are hydrogen bonds picks this. In fact peptide bonds are covalent and form the primary structure; the hydrogen bonds of secondary structure are additional, between the C=O and N–H groups of different peptide bonds.
Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding in regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the polypeptide backbone.

mcqs.q: In one region of a polypeptide there are two cysteines, an amino acid whose R-group contains a carboxyl group and an amino acid whose R-group contains an amine group. Which statement about the bonds these could form in the tertiary structure is correct?
options: The cysteines can form a covalent disulfide bond; the carboxyl and amine R-groups can form an ionic bond once the first has lost and the second has bound a hydrogen ion.
The cysteines can form a disulfide bridge, which is a strong hydrogen bond and so is broken by heating as easily as the other hydrogen bonds.
The carboxyl R-group becomes positively charged and the amine R-group becomes negatively charged, so the two attract and form an ionic bond.
The carboxyl and amine R-groups carry fixed charges, so an ionic bond between them is unaffected by any change in the pH of the solution.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four kinds of bond hold the fold (HL)
mcqs.explain: Pairs of cysteines form disulfide covalent bonds. The carboxyl group in an R-group becomes negatively charged by dissociation of a hydrogen ion and the amine group in an R-group becomes positively charged by binding one, and the two charged R-groups can then form an ionic bond.
rationales: Pairs of cysteines form disulfide covalent bonds. The carboxyl group in an R-group becomes negatively charged by dissociation of a hydrogen ion and the amine group in an R-group becomes positively charged by binding one, and the two charged R-groups can then form an ionic bond.

A student who lumps the disulfide bond with the weak interactions picks this. In fact it is a covalent bond between two sulfur atoms, far stronger than a hydrogen bond, and it survives heating and pH changes that break the other interactions.

A student who links acid with positive charge picks this. In fact the charges are the other way round: the carboxyl group loses a hydrogen ion and becomes negative, and the amine group binds one and becomes positive.

A student who thinks of protein charges like the fixed charges in sodium chloride picks this. In fact the charges depend on binding or dissociation of hydrogen ions, so a change in pH can remove them and break the ionic bond.

mcqs.q: A soluble globular enzyme was tested. A reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds cut its activity to 10%. Moving it from pH 7 to pH 4 cut its activity to 30%, and full activity returned when it was moved back to pH 7. Its polypeptide chain stayed intact in both experiments. What do these results show?
options: The loss of activity at pH 4 cannot involve ionic bonds, because the charges on R-groups do not change at all when the pH changes.
The tertiary structure depends on disulfide bonds and on ionic bonds between R-groups whose charges change reversibly with pH.
The reducing agent broke hydrogen bonds, since a disulfide bridge is the strongest type of hydrogen bond found in a protein.
Both treatments broke peptide bonds, and only the peptide bonds broken by the pH change were re-formed at pH 7.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four kinds of bond hold the fold (HL)
mcqs.explain: Breaking the disulfide bonds destroyed most of the activity, so they hold the tertiary structure. The pH change altered the charges on R-groups, which depend on binding or dissociation of hydrogen ions, disrupting ionic bonds; returning the pH restored the charges and the bonds.
rationales: A student who believes R-group charges are fixed picks this. In fact a fall in pH adds hydrogen ions to negatively charged carboxyl R-groups, removing their charge and breaking ionic bonds; restoring the pH restores the charges, which fits the recovery seen.

Breaking the disulfide bonds destroyed most of the activity, so they hold the tertiary structure. The pH change altered the charges on R-groups, which depend on binding or dissociation of hydrogen ions, disrupting ionic bonds; returning the pH restored the charges and the bonds.

A student who thinks a disulfide bridge is a kind of hydrogen bond picks this. In fact it is a covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteines, which is exactly why a reducing agent, not gentle heating, is needed to break it.

A student who thinks loss of activity means the chain has been broken picks this. In fact the polypeptide chain stayed intact in both experiments; the activity was lost because bonds holding the tertiary structure, not peptide bonds, were disrupted.

mcqs.q: A globular enzyme is dissolved in the cytoplasm, and an integral protein spans the plasma membrane. Where are the amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups located in each protein, and why?
options: Absent from the soluble enzyme, because a protein containing hydrophobic amino acids could not dissolve in water.
Throughout the whole of the integral protein, which must be hydrophobic on all of its surfaces to stay in the membrane.
In the enzyme's core and the integral protein's membrane region, because water molecules bond to each other and exclude non-polar R-groups.
In the enzyme's core and the integral protein's membrane region, because their non-polar R-groups repel the water molecules and push them away.
mcqs.specStatementText: Where polar and non-polar amino acids sit (HL)
mcqs.explain: In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of the globular protein, and integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids that sit in the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer. They end up there because water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and not to non-polar R-groups, which are therefore excluded from the water.
rationales: A student who judges solubility by adding up the amino acids picks this. In fact soluble globular proteins do contain hydrophobic amino acids; they are clustered in the core, away from water, while the surface is hydrophilic.

A student who thinks anything in a membrane must be hydrophobic all over picks this. In fact only the region within the bilayer has hydrophobic R-groups; the parts projecting into the aqueous solutions on either side are hydrophilic.

In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of the globular protein, and integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids that sit in the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer. They end up there because water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and not to non-polar R-groups, which are therefore excluded from the water.

A student who pictures hydrophobic groups pushing water away picks this. The locations are right but the mechanism is not: there is no repulsion; water molecules bond to each other and exclude non-polar groups, so hydrophobic R-groups end up away from water.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares insulin, collagen and haemoglobin?
options: All three are conjugated proteins, because each of them is built from more than one polypeptide chain.
The haem groups of haemoglobin are short polypeptides, so all three of these proteins are non-conjugated.
Insulin is a single polypeptide, so unlike collagen and haemoglobin it does not have quaternary structure.
Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein with haem groups; insulin and collagen are non-conjugated.
mcqs.explain: Haemoglobin is conjugated because each of its four polypeptides carries a haem group, a prosthetic group not made of amino acids. Insulin (two polypeptides) and collagen (three polypeptides) have quaternary structure but no prosthetic group, so they are non-conjugated.
rationales: A student who thinks conjugated means multi-chain picks this. In fact all three have quaternary structure, but only haemoglobin is conjugated, because it contains non-polypeptide haem groups; insulin and collagen consist of polypeptides only.

A student who assumes everything in a protein is made of amino acids picks this. In fact a haem group is not a polypeptide: it is a ring structure containing an iron ion, and its presence is what makes haemoglobin a conjugated protein.

A student who assumes a small hormone must be a single chain picks this. In fact insulin consists of two polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds, so it has quaternary structure and is the guide's example of a non-conjugated protein.

mcqs.q: Cryogenic electron microscopy has produced images of single protein molecules and of their interactions with other molecules. What does this illustrate about the role of technology in science?
options: Technology allows the imaging of structures that would be impossible to observe with the unaided senses, so new knowledge of proteins can be gained.
A light microscope with sufficient magnification could image single protein molecules, so the new technique is simply more convenient.
Molecules are far too small for any instrument to image, so protein structures can only be inferred, not observed directly.
Pictures of protein structure are artists' impressions based only on the amino acid sequence, so the images add nothing to knowledge.
mcqs.explain: This is the nature of science point in the guide: instruments extend observation far beyond what the senses can detect. Cryogenic electron microscopy has made the structures of single protein molecules and their interactions observable, producing knowledge that was previously unobtainable.

Cryogenic electron microscopy has made the structures of single protein molecules and their interactions observable, producing knowledge that was previously unobtainable.

A student who explains what a microscope can show by magnification alone picks this. In fact the wavelength of light limits resolution, so no amount of magnification lets a light microscope separate structures the size of a protein molecule.

A student who believes molecules can never be seen picks this. In fact cryogenic electron microscopy does image single protein molecules; it is an example of technology making observable what the unaided senses cannot detect.

A student who takes ribbon diagrams for drawings picks this. In fact such diagrams display structures that have been measured; cryogenic electron microscopy provides the observations from which the positions of atoms are determined.

mcqs.q: Protein X is compact and roughly spherical, dissolves in blood plasma and binds to a specific receptor on target cells. Protein Y forms long insoluble fibres with high tensile strength in tendons. Which statement correctly relates the form of each protein to its function?
options: Y is a polypeptide that has not folded up, and its lack of a defined structure is what allows it to form insoluble fibres.
X is globular like insulin, its precise shape fitting its receptor; Y is fibrous like collagen, its elongated shape suiting a structural role.
Y is a single very long polypeptide chain, and its tensile strength comes from the great length of that one chain alone.
X dissolves because it is built entirely from hydrophilic amino acids, and Y is insoluble because it is built entirely from hydrophobic amino acids.
mcqs.specStatementText: Globular and fibrous: shape fits job (HL)
mcqs.explain: X has the properties of a globular protein: compact, soluble and able to bind specifically, as insulin binds its receptor. Y has the properties of a fibrous protein: elongated, insoluble and strong, as collagen is in tendons. In each case the shape makes the protein suitable for its function.
rationales: A student who takes fibrous to mean unfolded picks this. In fact fibrous proteins such as collagen have a precise elongated structure, a triple helix of three polypeptides, and it is this organized structure that gives them strength.

X has the properties of a globular protein: compact, soluble and able to bind specifically, as insulin binds its receptor. Y has the properties of a fibrous protein: elongated, insoluble and strong, as collagen is in tendons. In each case the shape makes the protein suitable for its function.

A student who pictures a fibre as one thread picks this. In fact collagen consists of three polypeptides wound together into a triple helix, and many of these are linked into fibres; the winding and cross-linking, not chain length alone, give the strength.

A student who adds up the amino acids to judge solubility picks this. In fact a globular protein dissolves because its hydrophilic R-groups are on the surface while hydrophobic ones are in the core; solubility depends on the folded shape, not on the amino acids alone.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No amino acid is named as essential or non-essential anywhere in the concepts, misconceptions or items. Dietary requirements are tested only through the definitions (cannot be synthesized and must come from food; can be made from other amino acids) and through the reason a vegan diet needs attention, without naming which amino acids plant foods may lack.

No R-group is described by its chemical formula or by the name of the amino acid that carries it. R-groups are classified only as hydrophobic or hydrophilic, and hydrophilic ones only as polar or charged, acidic or basic, exactly as the guidance sets out.

Cysteine is the only amino acid named in connection with tertiary-structure bonding. Ionic bonding is described in terms of R-groups containing amine or carboxyl groups that gain or lose hydrogen ions, without naming the amino acids concerned; hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions are described only by the polarity of the R-groups involved.
